records.review_reason: Final deep-or-drop resolution: DROP from the verified radar for insufficient accessible evidence, not for false geographic relevance or suspected misconduct. The chapter is traceable bibliographically (DOI, authors, IGI Global book, chapter 7, pp. 201–224), and its author-side abstract explicitly discusses Morocco, but the publisher DOI/chapter full text could not be inspected; ResearchGate explicitly offers only a request-full-text option. The EurekaMag listing repeats chapter-level summary material and confirms citation identity rather than providing independently inspectable methodology. Two separate Moroccan supply-chain studies involving Boulitama and Sabiri (a 151-firm survey published by Vilnius University Press in 2026, and a 234-firm survey published in Polish Journal of Management Studies in 2025) corroborate that the researchers study Morocco-specific digital supply chains, but they are different publications with overlapping authors, not independent verification of this chapter’s analysis or asserted digital-technology effects. No independently tested chapter-specific Moroccan rollout, sustainability result, blockchain implementation or evidence protocol was available. The user requested definitive keep/drop; the chapter does not pass the full-text/substantive-method gate for Keep, so it is excluded as unverified, with no allegation of fabrication or influence activity.
records.decision_basis: DROP — Morocco and supply chains clearly match the abstract, but verified bibliographic identity and same-author adjacent empirical research cannot substitute for examination of this specific conceptual chapter and its evidence base. Insufficient chapter-level verification for promotion to the verified radar.

source_verification.basis: ResearchGate record names Boulitama and Sabiri, IGI Global edited book AI, Blockchain, and Emerging Technologies for Sustainable Supply Chains (2026), chapter 7, pp.201–224, and the exact DOI; an independent bibliography index lists the same title and pagination, while bookseller catalogues confirm the edited book and July 16 release. The fuller book-chapter title includes “Case of Morocco”, whereas the manifest title omits this subtitle. The accessible abstract claims a structured synthesis and Morocco-grounded logistic/industrial constraints, but ResearchGate explicitly says no full text is available; the DOI redirects to inaccessible services.igi-global.com. No unsupported claim of having read the chapter or observed effects is made. Final deeper verification (2026-11-16): IGI Global DOI resolution/full chapter remained inaccessible for chapter-level methodology review. A 2026 Vilnius University Press article by Boulitama and Sabiri, DOI 10.15388/Ekon.2026.105.1.3, reports a 151-firm Moroccan survey; a 2025 Polish Journal of Management Studies paper by Boulitama and Sabiri, DOI 10.17512/pjms.2025.32.1.04, reports a 234-company mixed-mode Moroccan survey. These are primary scholarly studies of closely related topics, but not independent validation of the chapter: they partly share the chapter authors and do not supply the missing chapter text or separate ESG/blockchain impact evidence. Source identity and relevance are supported, but chapter-specific research integrity and strength of evidence remain unverified. The Drop is exclusion on an evidence-threshold basis, not an accusation of illegitimacy.

records.review_reason: Final deep-or-drop resolution: DROP from the verified radar on methodological quality, not because the subject or Albanian geography is irrelevant. The full 7-page publisher PDF was inspected including p.69 research methodology, p.70 readiness pie chart and p.71 ESG impact graph. The paper describes its 15%/45%/40% technology-provider segments as adapted from Tavanxhiu et al. (2026) but does not give a fresh sample, denominator, or audit trail for converting the original 17.7%/43.5%/38.8% in Godolja et al. (2025) into these figures. The paper’s expert-derived potential scores (7.5–9.2 on a 0–10 scale) do not disclose number or selection of experts, questions, weighting, calibration, or uncertainty estimates. Its own limitations concede reliance on general assessments instead of comprehensive original data for readiness, and the broad benefits asserted are scenario/technology potentials rather than measured Albanian hotel outcomes. Publisher article and PDF date the publication June 30, 2026, rather than manifest June 1, 2026. An independent peer-reviewed 2025 provider study with N=1,821 validates a broad Albania-specific readiness challenge, not this manuscript’s reworked figures or AI-ESG scores. No plagiarism/fabrication/propaganda allegation is made; the candidate is excluded because its prominent quantitative findings cannot be validated to the radar standard.
records.decision_basis: DROP — authentic Albania-specific AI-tourism article, but derivative sector-readiness percentages and un-auditable expert ESG scores are central to its results; they do not meet the verification standard. Prefer the separate 2025 primary provider survey as a new, distinct candidate.

source_verification.basis: The European Journal of Business and Management (IISTE) article DOI, authors, 7-page PDF and Albanian sector focus match the record. The manifest supplies 2026-06-01 but journal page and PDF both print June 30, 2026. The article says its readiness segments were adapted from Tavanxhiu et al. (2026) and that numerical ESG potential scores are expert-derived; it also admits segments are based on general assessments, not comprehensive primary survey data. The publisher openly advertises a paid peer-review process and an approximately 10-day review cycle, a quality-control concern rather than proof of fabrication. Separate primary empirical work by Godolja et al. (2025) reports N=1,821 providers and segment percentages of 17.7/43.5/38.8, similar in pattern but not identical to this article’s 15/45/40 rounding. No independent assessment of this paper’s 7.5–9.2 scores was established. Final recheck (2026-11-16): full PDF pages 69–71 inspected directly. Page 69 labels the work exploratory/descriptive, bases provider segmentation on Tavanxhiu et al. (2026) and invokes an expert-derived AI impact index without a detailed scoring method. Page 70 charts provider group shares 15.0%/45.0%/40.0%; page 71 reports 7.5–9.2 impact assessments with no auditable expert protocol or confidence intervals. The separate 2025 Tourism and Hospitality study by Godolja, Tavanxhiu and Sevrani reports N=1,821 and actual segment values 17.7%/43.5%/38.8%; it supports the broad context but not the source article’s numerical ESG claims. Drop reflects insufficient methodological evidence, not a finding that the journal is a fabricated enterprise.
